result.summary: Pausanias traces the Eurypontid line of Spartan kings from Procles to Archidamus, son of Zeuxidamus. He notes wars with Argos, the loss of Demaratus's throne after Aristo's careless remark, and Leotychides' exile. The chapter ends with Archidamus's invasions of Attica and the Peloponnesian War.

scenes.title: Early Eurypontid kings and wars
scenes.summary: Pausanias lists the kings from Procles to Agesicles and the wars with Argos, Tegea and Messenia during their reigns.

scenes.title: Aristo, Demaratus and exile
scenes.summary: Aristo doubts his son Demaratus because of the early birth. Demaratus later loses his kingdom and goes to Darius in Persia.
scenes.stakes: Demaratus loses his kingdom through his father's rash word and Cleomenes' hatred.

scenes.title: Leotychides and Archidamus
scenes.summary: Leotychides fights at Mycale, takes bribes in Thessaly and flees to Tegea. His grandson Archidamus ravages Attica and takes Plataea as the Peloponnesian War begins.
scenes.stakes: Leotychides faces trial at Sparta; Greece is shaken by war.

alias_notes.explanation: The Proclid royal family was renamed after Eurypon.

notable_quotes.reason: Pausanias's judgment that the Peloponnesian War ruined Greece, leaving it ripe for Philip.

analysis.text: Pausanias traces how personal flaws and quarrels, like Aristo's hasty remark, shape the fate of dynasties and states.
The chapter reflects the Spartan dual kingship and the Peloponnesian War as the turning point toward Macedonian domination.

language_notes.text: Agiadæ: the Spartan royal house descended from Agis, son of Eurysthenes. Sparta had two kings at once, from two families.
Proclidæ and Eurypontidæ are names of the same royal house, using the Greek patronymic ending -idai, 'descendants of'.
'Slice the district off from Arcadia' means to cut Tegea's territory away and annex it. The 'beguiling oracle' misled the Spartans into thinking they would succeed.
'Paid the penalty' means they were punished by the Argives, who destroyed the Asinæans' land and drove them out.
Thyrea was a border district disputed by Argos and Sparta; the contest over it is the famous battle of the Champions.
'Evacuated the Peloponnese' means the defeated Messenians left the peninsula as exiles.
The ephors were five annually elected Spartan magistrates who oversaw the kings and sat with them in council.
In the Iliad, Hera hastened Eurystheus' birth to seven months, so a seven-month child could be legitimate. Aristo overlooked this precedent.
The Pisistratidæ were the sons of the Athenian tyrant Pisistratus; Sparta under Cleomenes helped expel Hippias in 510 BC.
Mycale, in 479 BC, was the Greek victory over the Persians on the Ionian coast, fought on the same campaign as Plataea.
The Aleuadæ were the ruling aristocratic family of Larissa in Thessaly, who had favored Persia.
A suppliant sought protection at a sanctuary, which made him legally inviolable there.
Sthenelaidas, ephor in 432 BC, urged the Spartan assembly to vote for war against Athens.
Philip II of Macedon defeated the Greeks at Chaeronea in 338 BC, ending their independence.

context_notes.text: Teleclus was an Agiad king. Pausanias elsewhere tells how he was killed at a sanctuary on the Laconian-Messenian border.
Theopompus is best known as a Spartan king during the first Messenian War, which Pausanias treats in his Messenia book.
Long peace in these reigns contrasts with the earlier wars. Pausanias is simply moving through the Eurypontid list to Agesicles.
Demaratus fled to Persia around 491 BC, and Darius gave him lands. His descendants held towns in the Troad.
Archidamus led the Spartan invasions of Attica in the early Peloponnesian War, beginning in 431 BC. Plataea fell in 427 BC.

literary_notes.text: The oracle's promise tempts the Spartans into a campaign that fails, so the hopeful prophecy proves deceptive.
Theopompus's grief outweighs even old age as a reason to abstain, giving a brief human touch to the king.
Aristo's hasty doubt of his son, which ignores a famous legend, ironically costs that son the throne.
Greece is likened to a building shaken to its foundation or to rotten timber, picturing decay before Philip's conquest.
